title: The householder's path, closed
hook: work, money, family, friends, body, age: one bedside talk holds them all
tomorrow: everyone knows they'll die. so why think about it on purpose?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ageing well: Mahakassapa, old and still practicing, into old age. Today the householder's path closes, at one sickbed.
screen: `INTO OLD AGE.` → `THE PATH CLOSES AT A SICKBED.`

segments.voice: Hospital waiting rooms run on the same quiet talk under the beeping: who pays the bills, who picks up the kids, what happens to the house. An old story sits right inside that talk. A householder known as Nakula's father lies badly sick, and he isn't worried about dying. He's worried about his wife. Will she manage the money? The children? Will she marry again? Will she stop going to hear the Buddha? She leans in close, and answers every worry, one by one.
screen: `WHO PAYS? WHO PICKS UP THE KIDS?` → `A SICK MAN, WORRIED FOR HIS WIFE.` → `SHE LEANS IN.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Anguttara Nikaya, and it's mostly her talking. Don't die worried, she tells him; the Blessed One says dying with worry is painful. Then, worry by worry. The money: I'm good at spinning cotton and carding wool; I can keep the children fed. The marriage: you know I won't take another husband. The teaching: I'll want to see the Buddha and the monks more, not less. And her own practice: she keeps the precepts, she has found calm in her mind, she's gone beyond doubt in the teaching. If you're unsure, she says, go ask the Blessed One. Then the twist. Nakula's father gets better. He gets up from his sickbed, still weak, leaning on a stick, and goes to the Buddha himself. The Buddha tells him he's fortunate: Nakula's mother is his counselor and teacher, full of kindness for his good. Now hold her speech up to the light. Work is in it, the spinning. Money, the children's food. Family, the marriage. Friends, the community around the Buddha. The body, sick in that bed, and age, the long life they've shared. Every room of the householder's path is in one bedside talk, and in every room the practice was already there. Not on a cushion somewhere else. In the cotton, in a promise, in a steady voice next to a frightened man.
screen: `DON'T DIE WORRIED.` · `WORRY BY WORRY, SHE ANSWERS.` · `HE GETS UP, LEANING ON A STICK.` · `EVERY ROOM OF THE HOUSEHOLD.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Name one room of your life where the practice feels thinnest right now: work, money, family, friends, or the body. Bring to mind one ordinary moment there this week, the hard email or the tense dinner. Then choose one small thing to carry into it, a breath before you answer or a gentler word, and rest with that choice until the bell.
The householder's path: the Buddha's teaching lived inside work, money, family, friends, body and age, not away from them. Today it closes.
Your line: practice is everywhere, even beside a sickbed. A new stretch of the path begins tomorrow. Day sixteen twenty-five, closed.

screen: `DAY 1625 COUNTS.` → `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH · COMPLETE.` → `TOMORROW: WHY THINK ABOUT DEATH ON PURPOSE?`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell lay students the story of Nakula's parents to show that the path can be walked in married and working life; temples in many countries hold teachings for householders alongside programs for monks and nuns.

fork.setup: your dad is laid up after surgery and keeps asking how the family will manage. you're scared too. what does Nakula's mother do in your place?
options: change the subject to something cheerful, so he stops thinking about it.
answer each worry plainly and calmly, one at a time.
tell him worrying is bad for his recovery and he should stop.
fork.reveal: she doesn't dodge or scold. she takes each worry, money, marriage, teaching, and answers it, and the Buddha calls her his counselor and teacher.

original.note: Pali: householder, the head of a household; the word the suttas use for lay followers like Nakula's father.

trapdoor: what you thought: the householder's path is the easy version for people who can't be monks.
what it means: work, money, family, friends, body and age are where a lay follower practices; Nakula's mother shows all of them at one sickbed.
what a scholar hears: AN 6.16 (Nakulapita Sutta) gives her answers worry by worry, and the Buddha praises her as her husband's counselor and teacher.
guess: the Buddha's path lived in ordinary home life
a monk's path, walked only inside a monastery
the road a family takes to a temple festival

chat.says: visiting ông's old friend bác Hùng in the hospital tomorrow. that's not practice, just being nice, right?
options: It is practice. A steady voice at a sickbed was Nakula's mother's practice.
Right. Practice is the sitting part; visits are just good manners.
Only if you meditate there first. That's what makes a visit count.
chat.meaning: Nakula's mother practiced at her husband's sickbed, answering his worries calmly. Practice isn't only on a cushion.

tie.story: Nakula's mother answered her sick husband's worries one by one, and the Buddha called her his teacher.
tie.friend: Mai's visit to bác Hùng with ông is practice too, if she brings a steady, kind presence.

Mahakassapa.meaning: a senior disciple of the Buddha who practiced into old age

Anguttara Nikaya.meaning: the collection of the Buddha's discourses arranged by number

Blessed One.meaning: a title for the Buddha used throughout the suttas

precepts.meaning: the five training rules lay Buddhists undertake

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.16 (Nakulapita Sutta: Nakula's mother answers her sick husband's worries; he recovers and the Buddha praises her)

notes: AN 6.16 paraphrased: her assurances (spinning cotton and carding wool to support the children; not remarrying; wanting to see the Blessed One and the Sangha more; keeping the precepts, gaining inner serenity, going beyond doubt) and the Buddha's praise of her as counselor and teacher. The sutta's number of years of celibate married life is left out on purpose (claims rule). Confirm the order and wording.
Nakulapita also appears on day 1619 (SN 22.1, sick in body, not in mind); this day uses a different sutta (AN 6.16) and a different angle (his wife's answers). A light callback in recall only.
Story shape: one scene told from the middle; the teach closes Block E by naming its rooms (work, money, family, friends, body, age) in her speech.

v3 storyline (Mai, days 1625-1638): Ông Thanh's old friend from the bonsai club, bác Hùng (fictional), is in the hospital; over two weeks he dies, Mai goes with Ông to the funeral and the temple memorial, draws his portrait for the altar, and Ông receives his juniper.
